title: Homomorphisms from smooth connected affine groups to abelian varieties vanish
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $L/k$ be a smooth connected affine group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism, def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions], not necessarily commutative, where affine means isomorphic to the spectrum of a commutative ring [def-pc-scheme]. Let $A/k$ be an abelian variety [def-sc-abelian-variety]. Every homomorphism $f:L\to A$ of $k$-group schemes is the zero homomorphism: $f=e_A\circ(L\to\operatorname{Spec}k)$, where $e_A$ is the identity section of $A$. This includes $L=1$ and $A=1$.

source.place: Proposition 8.1(b) and Example 8.4, printed p.149, together with the homomorphism image factorization of Theorem 5.39, printed pp.108--109. Also Conrad, Semistable Reduction for Abelian Varieties, Example 2.4, printed pp.2--3. No Stacks tag states this vanishing assertion.

proof.text: The definition of an abelian variety makes $A$ proper, hence separated and of finite type over $k$. The group-scheme separatedness lemma makes $L$ separated too. Apply the homomorphism theorem to $f$: obtain $f=i\circ q$, with $q:L\to I$ faithfully flat and finitely presented, $i:I\hookrightarrow A$ a closed immersion of finite-type group schemes, and $N=\ker f=\ker q$ a closed normal subgroup of $L$. The theorem identifies $I$ with the fppf sheaf quotient $L/N$.

source.place: Theorem 5.39 and Remark 5.40, printed p.108; Proposition 8.1(b) and Example 8.4, printed p.149

proof.text: Write $L=\operatorname{Spec}R$. Since $N\hookrightarrow L$ is a closed immersion, the affine characterization of a closed immersion writes $N=\operatorname{Spec}(R/J)$ for an ideal $J$; thus $N$ is affine. Apply the affine normal quotient theorem to $N\triangleleft L$. It supplies an affine finite-type group scheme $Q=L/N$, with quotient map $r:L\to Q$. Because $L$ is smooth, $Q$ is smooth. Because $k$ is already algebraically closed and $L$ is connected, $L$ is geometrically connected in the theorem's stated sense (connected after algebraic closure); hence $Q$ is geometrically connected, in particular connected. There is no smoothness assumption on $N$.

source.place: Theorem 5.39 and Remark 5.40, printed p.108; Proposition 8.1(b) and Example 8.4, printed p.149

proof.text: The quotient descriptions identify $I$ and $Q$ compatibly with their maps from $L$. Explicitly, on commutative $k$-algebras both are sheafifications of the same presheaf $R\mapsto L(R)/N(R)$. The sheafification universal property gives maps in both directions; their composites are identities by uniqueness. These natural maps on affine test schemes extend to all test schemes: cover a test scheme by affine opens, map the restrictions, and glue the resulting morphisms; naturality on affine opens in intersections gives compatibility. Uniqueness of gluing is the representable descent lemma, applied to the Zariski cover (an fpqc covering). Yoneda then gives inverse scheme morphisms $I\simeq Q$ over $k$. Consequently $I$ is affine, smooth and connected. This is the uniqueness argument of Milne Remark 5.40, not an assertion that a faithfully flat quotient of an arbitrary affine scheme is affine.

source.place: Theorem 5.39 and Remark 5.40, printed p.108; Proposition 8.1(b) and Example 8.4, printed p.149

proof.text: The closed immersion $i:I\hookrightarrow A$, with $A$ proper over $k$, makes $I$ proper over $k$ by the closed-immersion properness lemma. Since $I$ is also affine, the proper-affine finiteness lemma makes $I\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ finite. Thus $I=\operatorname{Spec}B$ for a finite-dimensional commutative $k$-algebra $B$.

source.place: Tag 01W5, lemma-closed-immersion-proper; Tag 01W3, lemma-composition-proper; Tag 01WN, lemma-finite-proper; Milne Example 8.4, printed p.149

proof.text: Smoothness of $I$ over the field $k$ gives geometrically reduced fibres by the smooth-fibre lemma; the fibre over the sole point of $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is $I$ itself. In particular $I$ is reduced, so $B=\Gamma(I,\mathcal O_I)$ is reduced: a nilpotent section has zero germ in every reduced local ring and hence is zero. The identity section gives a $k$-algebra map $B\to k$, so $1\ne0$ in $B$ and $I$ is nonempty. Since $I$ is connected, the idempotent criterion says that $B$ has only the idempotents $0,1$. Apply the finite reduced algebra lemma over the algebraically closed field $k$: the structure map $k\to B$ is bijective. Its inverse is the map of the identity section, since the latter is a retraction of the structure map. Therefore the structure map $p_I:I\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ and $e_I$ are inverse isomorphisms.

source.place: Tag 056T, lemma-smooth-geometrically-normal; Tag 0BUG, lemma-proper-geometrically-reduced-global-sections, proof (2); Milne Example 8.4, printed p.149

proof.text: Finally $\mathrm{id}_I=e_I\circ p_I$, and $i\circ e_I=e_A$ because $i$ is a group homomorphism. Hence $f=i\circ q=i\circ e_I\circ p_I\circ q=e_A\circ p_L$, where $p_L:L\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is the structure map. This proves equality of scheme morphisms and therefore of group-scheme homomorphisms, including on nonreduced test schemes. The same calculation covers $L=1$ and $A=1$.

Its six steps follow Milne, Algebraic Groups: Theorem 5.39 and Remark 5.40, Proposition 8.1(b) and Example 8.4 (pp.108 and 149, checked in the PDF). Step checks: (1) The hypotheses of the homomorphism-factorization node hold: A is proper, hence separated and of finite type, and L is separated by the group-separatedness lemma. (2) N is affine because it is a closed subscheme of the affine L. The affine normal-quotient node then gives Q affine, smooth and geometrically connected, using that k is algebraically closed. (3) I and Q are identified because both represent the same fppf quotient, via sheafification, Zariski gluing of maps through the fpqc representable-descent lemma (a Zariski cover is an fpqc covering) and Yoneda; marking this step elementary is acceptable. The two nodes word their fppf coverings slightly differently; I accepted this because both mean the same fppf quotient. (4) I is proper by clause (c) of the closed-immersion lemma, and affine by step 3, so it is finite. (5) I is smooth, hence reduced, nonzero (it has an identity section) and connected, hence has only trivial idempotents. The finite reduced algebra lemma then gives B=k, and e_I is inverse to p_I. (6) f=e_A∘p_L follows by composing the maps. Edge cases checked: L=1, A=1, noncommutative L, nonreduced kernel, alpha_p and mu_2.
